title.text: Gradient descent: training is walking downhill on the loss, one step at a time

objects.text: How does a model with millions or billions of numbers find good values for all of them?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 10 of 18  |  Calculus and optimisation
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes: Welcome to Session 10. Last time you learned the chain rule, which gives the gradient of the loss. Today we use that gradient. A model with billions of numbers cannot be solved with a formula, so it is trained by taking many small steps downhill. That one idea, gradient descent, is how language models are trained. We will do the arithmetic by hand, then watch it run.

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can do three things. First, apply the update rule by hand: the new w equals the old w minus the learning rate times the gradient. Second, say what goes wrong when the learning rate is too small or too large, and what mini-batches, momentum and Adam change.

Third, write the loop yourself for a line fit, in Python or as one spreadsheet row per step, and compare the loss curves for four learning rates.

title.text:
Your two hours: learn the
update rule, then watch it run

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures and hand calculations first. Then the lab: a loop in Python or one row per step.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes recall the chain rule from Session 9 and ask the question of the day. Then thirty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptop: the update rule, the learning rate, batches, momentum and Adam. After a break comes the lab, forty-five minutes, where you write gradient descent yourself for a line fit.

The last fifteen minutes show where it appears in ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and other AI, then an exit check.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Use the chain rule: what is the derivative of y = (3x plus 1) squared with respect to x?
2.  A function takes 3 inputs and gives 2 outputs. What shape is its Jacobian matrix?
3.  Why does backpropagation need the chain rule?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 9. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Use the chain rule: what is the derivative of y = (3x plus 1) squared with respect to x? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. It is 6(3x + 1): the outer derivative 2(3x + 1) multiplied by the inner derivative 3.

Question two. A function takes 3 inputs and gives 2 outputs. What shape is its Jacobian matrix? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Two rows and three columns: one row for each output and one column for each input.

Question three. Why does backpropagation need the chain rule? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. A network is a function of functions, so the slope of the loss for an early weight is a product of the slopes along the path to the loss.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 9

rows.text: Use the chain rule: what is the derivative of y = (3x plus 1) squared with respect to x?
It is 6(3x + 1): the outer derivative 2(3x + 1) multiplied by the inner derivative 3.
A function takes 3 inputs and gives 2 outputs. What shape is its Jacobian matrix?
Two rows and three columns: one row for each output and one column for each input.
Why does backpropagation need the chain rule?
A network is a function of functions, so the slope of the loss for an early weight is a product of the slopes along the path to the loss.

objects.text: Check your answers. If one surprised you, look at Session 9 before the lab.

slides.notes:
For y equals three x plus one, all squared, the chain rule gives six times three x plus one. The outer derivative is two times the bracket, and the inner derivative is three. A function with three inputs and two outputs has a Jacobian with two rows and three columns.

And backpropagation uses the chain rule because a network is a function of functions, so the slope for an early weight is a product of local slopes. Today those slopes finally get used. If you got all three, you are ready.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Repeatedly changing the parameters a little in the direction that lowers the loss.
The size of each step. We write it as the Greek letter eta; some books write alpha.
An epoch is one pass through all the training rows. A mini-batch is a small group of rows used for one step.
A running memory of past gradients that smooths the path and speeds it up.
An optimiser (Kingma and Ba, 2014) that gives each parameter its own step size.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Gradient descent. Repeatedly changing the parameters a little in the direction that lowers the loss.

Learning rate (eta). The size of each step. We write it as the Greek letter eta; some books write alpha.

Epoch and mini-batch. An epoch is one pass through all the training rows. A mini-batch is a small group of rows used for one step.

Momentum. A running memory of past gradients that smooths the path and speeds it up.

Adam. An optimiser (Kingma and Ba, 2014) that gives each parameter its own step size.

title.text:
Training a model means
walking downhill on the loss

objects.alt: Training a model means walking downhill on the loss

objects.text: The loss L measures how wrong the model is. Training lowers it.

runs.text: The curve shows the loss for each value of one parameter w.
At the start the slope is negative, so the loss falls if w grows. We step that way.
The bottom of the curve is the best value of w.

slides.notes:
Look at the curve. The horizontal axis is one parameter of the model, called w. The vertical axis is the loss, a single number for how wrong the model is. We start at the gold dot on the left. There the slope is negative, which means the loss goes down if we increase w.

So we take a step to the right, then measure the slope again, and step again. The bottom of the bowl is the best w. This walk downhill is called gradient descent. Why do we need the slope to decide which way to go?

title.text:
The update rule: new w equals old w
minus the learning rate times the gradient

objects.alt: The update rule: new w equals old w minus the learning rate times the gradient

rows.text: The parameter we improve. The arrow means: replace the old value. Bold w is the column of all the parameters (Session 8 also calls it theta).
The size of each step. Some books write alpha.
The slope of the loss with respect to w (a derivative).
The gradient: the column of all partial derivatives (Session 8).

objects.text: Worked: w = 0 - 0.1 × (-6) = 0.6. The minus sign moves w the way that lowers the loss.

slides.notes:
This one line is what every training run repeats. The new w equals the old w minus eta times the slope of the loss. Eta is the learning rate, the size of each step. Try it on the bowl from the last slide, where the loss is w minus three, squared.

At w equals zero the slope is minus six. So the new w is zero minus point one times minus six, which is 0.6. With many parameters we write the same thing with the gradient, the column of partial derivatives from Session 8. The minus sign matters: the slope points uphill, so we step the other way.

title.text:
Five steps by hand on the bowl (w minus 3) squared
with eta = 0.1: the steps shrink by themselves

rows.text: w after = w before minus 0.1 × slope

objects.text: Each step closes one fifth of the remaining gap to 3. The best value is w = 3, where the slope is 0.

slides.notes:
Five steps by hand. Start at w equals zero. The slope is minus six, so the new w is 0.6. Next, the slope at 0.6 is -4.8, so the new w is 1.08. The steps shrink: as w approaches three the slope gets smaller, so the step gets smaller without us changing anything.

After five steps w is 2.017, close to the best value of three. Each step closes one fifth of the remaining gap, because point one times two is one fifth. Take your calculator and check the third row yourself.

title.text:
A line fit becomes a loss: a straight-line
model and its mean squared error

objects.alt: A line fit becomes a loss: a straight-line model and its mean squared error

rows.text: Centred distance of row i: distance minus the average 4.5 km.
Actual fare and predicted fare of row i, in thousand UGX.
Intercept (the fare at the average distance) and slope (thousand UGX per km).

objects.text: Start: the loss is the mean of y squared, 52.11. Centred x adds up to 0, so ∂L/∂w does not involve b.

slides.notes:
A real problem: fit a line to eight boda boda trips. The numbers are illustrative, made up to show the arithmetic. The input x is the trip distance minus the average of 4.5 kilometres, and y is the fare in thousand shillings. The model is y hat equals b plus w times x, and the loss is the mean squared error.

With w and b at zero every prediction is zero, so the loss is the mean of y squared, 52.11. Why centre?

The centred distances add up to zero, so the slope for w stops depending on b, and one learning rate suits both. This is the Session 8 gradient again, on new data.

title.text:
The gradient of the line-fit loss
has one entry for w and one for b

objects.alt: The gradient of the line-fit loss has one entry for w and one for b

rows.text: How fast the loss changes when w changes (a partial derivative, Session 8).
How fast the loss changes when b changes.
The error of row i. Positive means too high.
Add over the rows, then multiply by 2/n.
2/8 = 0.25; sum of error × x = -44.10; sum of errors = -54.4

objects.text: Both slopes are negative here, so the update raises both w and b.

slides.notes:
The gradient has two entries, one for each parameter. Both come from the chain rule of Session 9. The outer function is the square, whose derivative is two times the error. The inner function is b plus w times x, whose derivative with respect to w is x, and with respect to b is one.

So the slope for w is two over n times the sum of error times x, and the slope for b is two over n times the sum of the errors. At our start the two values are -11.025 and -13.600. Both are negative, so both parameters should grow.

title.text:
Step 1 of the line fit by hand,
starting from w = 0 and b = 0

slides.notes:
Step one with every number written out. With w and b at zero, each prediction is zero, so the error is minus y. The last column multiplies each error by x, and the two sums sit under the table. The slope for w is two over eight, that is point two five, times -44.10, which gives -11.025.

The slope for b is point two five times -54.4, which gives -13.600. With eta equal to point one, the new w is 1.1025 and the new b is 1.3600. This is exactly the first row of the spreadsheet lab.

title.text:
Mean, half-sum and full-sum squared error
share one minimum; only the step size changes

objects.alt: Mean, half-sum and full-sum squared error share one minimum; only the step size changes

rows.text: Loss and slope for w at w = 0, b = 0.
n/2 = 4 times the MSE, and so is every slope.
n = 8 times the MSE, and so is every slope.
The same for all three: multiplying by a positive number moves no minimum.

objects.text: Same step, smaller eta: 0.1 with MSE equals 0.025 with the half sum or 0.0125 with SSE.

slides.notes:
Books and libraries write the squared-error loss in three ways, and you will meet all three in this course. Today we use the mean. Session 11 uses one half of the sum, and Session 12 uses the plain sum plus a penalty. They differ only by a constant factor.

With our eight trips the half sum is four times the mean, and the full sum is eight times the mean, so every slope is four or eight times larger too. The bottom of the bowl does not move, so the best line is the same. Only the step size changes, which is why the learning rate must shrink by the same factor.

title.text:
The learning rate sets the size of each step: too
small crawls, good arrives, too large overshoots

objects.alt: The learning rate sets the size of each step: too small crawls, good arrives, too large overshoots

objects.text: Each panel: L(w) = (w - 3)^2, starting at w = 0. Dots are w after each step; arrows are the steps.

slides.notes:
The learning rate is the one setting you must get right. On the left, eta is point zero one: every step is tiny, and after five steps we have barely moved. In the middle, eta is point one: the steps start big and shrink as the slope flattens, so we arrive at the bottom.

On the right, eta is one point one: the step is so large that we jump past the bottom and land higher up the other side. The next jump is bigger again, and the loss grows instead of falling. In a real run you see only the loss, never this picture.

title.text:
The same three learning rates
as numbers: w after each step

objects.text: The loss at step 0 is 9 in all three columns. With eta = 1.0 exactly, w would bounce between 0 and 6 forever.

slides.notes:
The numbers behind the picture. With eta point zero one, w creeps from zero to 0.288 in five steps, and the loss is still 7.354. With eta point one, w reaches 2.017 and the loss is 0.966. With eta one point one, w goes to 6.6, then -1.32, then 8.184.

It swings further from three every time, and the loss grows to 55.726. The rule of thumb: if the loss goes up, the learning rate is too large.

title.text:
Batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent
use different numbers of rows for each step

objects.alt: Batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent use different numbers of rows for each step

objects.text: Gold squares: the rows used for one gradient. An epoch is one pass through all 8 rows.

slides.notes:
So far every gradient used all eight rows. That is called batch gradient descent, one step per epoch. With millions of rows it is slow, because one step needs a pass over everything. Stochastic gradient descent, SGD, uses a single row per step, so eight steps per epoch here.

Each step is cheap, but the path is noisy, because one row is a poor guide. The compromise is the mini-batch: a small group of rows, here four, so two steps per epoch. Its gradient is a noisy estimate of the full one, and in library manuals the name SGD usually means this version.

title.text:
Momentum keeps a running memory of
past gradients, which smooths a zigzag path

objects.alt: Momentum keeps a running memory of past gradients, which smooths a zigzag path

objects.text: Same valley, same start. Momentum damps the sideways swings that make plain descent zigzag.

slides.notes:
Here the loss is a long narrow valley. The gradient points mostly across the valley rather than along it, so plain gradient descent zigzags and makes slow progress along the floor. Momentum adds a memory. Sideways gradients point one way, then the other, so they largely cancel in the memory.

Gradients along the valley all point the same way, so they add up. The result on the right is a smoother, faster path, because each step carries some speed from the steps before it.

title.text:
The momentum velocity is a
decaying sum of past gradients

objects.alt: The momentum velocity is a decaying sum of past gradients

rows.text: The velocity: a running total of past gradients, each older one counted less. It starts at 0. (Adam's v, which follows, is a different thing.)
The momentum coefficient, between 0 and 1. A common choice is 0.9.

objects.text: Steady gradient 2: u = 2, then 0.9 × 2 + 2 = 3.8, then 0.9 × 3.8 + 2 = 5.42. It grows towards 20.

slides.notes:
This is the momentum update, in the form used by common libraries. The velocity, written u, is beta times the old velocity plus the new gradient. The weight then moves by eta times u. We use the letter u so it is not confused with the v of Adam, which comes next.

Take a gradient that stays at two. The first u is two. The second is point nine times two plus two, which is 3.8. The third is point nine times 3.8 plus two, which is 5.42. The velocity keeps growing while the gradient keeps its sign, up to ten times the gradient when beta is point nine. If the gradient flips sign, the velocity shrinks.

title.text:
Adam divides the average gradient by its typical
size, so each parameter steps by about alpha

objects.alt: Adam divides the average gradient by its typical size, so each parameter steps by about alpha

rows.text: Running averages of the gradients (like momentum) and of the squared gradients. Both start at 0.
The corrected averages. β1ᵗ is β1 to the power t, and t is the step number.
Adam's learning rate (the paper writes alpha).
A tiny number that avoids dividing by zero.

slides.notes:
Adam, published by Kingma and Ba in 2014, keeps two running averages for each parameter. The first, m, averages the gradients, which works like momentum. The second, v, averages the squared gradients, which measures how large the gradients typically are. Both start at zero, so the first values are too small, and the correction divides by one minus beta to the power t to fix that.

The step is alpha times m hat over the root of v hat. When the gradient is steady, top and bottom have the same size, so every parameter moves by about alpha, whatever the size of its gradient.

title.text:
Adam by hand: three steps on
the same bowl, starting at w = 0

objects.text: alpha = 0.1, beta1 = 0.9, beta2 = 0.999, epsilon = 1e-8. Subtracted = alpha × m-hat / (sqrt(v-hat) + epsilon). Subtracting a negative amount moves w to the right.

slides.notes:
Three Adam steps with real numbers. At step one the gradient is minus six. The average m is point one times minus six, which is -0.6000. The average v is point zero zero one times thirty-six, which is 0.0360. After the correction, m hat is minus six and the square root of v hat is six, so the amount subtracted is alpha times minus one.

Subtracting minus point one moves w up to 0.1000. At step two the gradient is -5.8000 and the step is again almost exactly alpha. By step three w is 0.2996. The steps stay near alpha even though the slope shrinks.

title.text:
A convex loss has a single bottom, while
a network loss can have several dips

objects.alt: A convex loss has a single bottom, while a network loss can have several dips

objects.text: Left: a convex loss, one bowl. Right: several dips. A local minimum is a dip that is not the lowest.

slides.notes:
Convexity tells us how safe gradient descent is. A convex loss, on the left, is a single bowl. From any start, walking downhill reaches the one bottom. The mean squared error of a line fit is convex. On the right is a loss with several dips. A dip that is lower than its neighbours but not the lowest is a local minimum.

Gradient descent can stop there, depending on where it started. The loss of a neural network is not convex. Even so, published experience is that large networks usually train well with the methods in this session, though we cannot prove that from this picture.

title.text:
A learning-rate schedule
changes eta during training

objects.alt: A learning-rate schedule changes eta during training

objects.text: A schedule gives a different learning rate at each step.

runs.text: Grey: constant, or cut in steps.
Red: warm-up to the peak over 100 steps, then a smooth cosine fall to 0 at step 1000. Peak 0.001: 0.0005 at steps 50 and 550.

slides.notes:
A learning-rate schedule changes eta as training goes on. The grey dashed line is a constant rate. The grey solid line cuts the rate in steps. The red line is warm-up followed by cosine decay. In warm-up the rate rises from zero to its peak over the first hundred steps, because the first gradients can be unreliable.

Then it falls along half a cosine wave, so the late steps are small and settle into a minimum. With an illustrative peak of point zero zero one, step fifty and step five hundred and fifty both have half the peak, 0.0005. Large steps help early; small steps help late.

title.text:
Four ways gradient descent goes
wrong, and how each one shows itself

rows.text: The loss goes up, or becomes nan (not a number)
Divide eta by 3 or 10 and run again
The loss falls, but so slowly that it looks flat
Multiply eta by 3 or 10, or train for more steps
The loss climbs from the first step
Use w - eta × gradient, with the minus sign
One learning rate is too large for one parameter and too small for another
Centre (and, with several inputs, scale) the inputs. The lab centres the distance.

slides.notes:
A learning rate that is too large shows as a loss that goes up or turns into nan, which means not a number. Divide eta by three or ten. Too small, and the loss falls so slowly it looks flat, so increase eta or run longer. A wrong sign means you add the gradient instead of subtracting it, and you walk uphill from step one.

Inputs on very different scales make one learning rate wrong for some parameter. With centred distances our w is stable for any eta below 0.19; with raw distances the limit drops to about 0.038.

title.text:
Momentum and Adam both smooth
the steps, but Adam also rescales them

objects.alt: gear

objects.text: SGD with momentum

runs.text: One learning rate eta for all parameters
Remembers past gradients
Needs eta tuned with care

objects.alt: robot

objects.text: Adam

runs.text: A separate effective step for each parameter
Remembers past gradients and their typical size
Works with the default settings in many cases

objects.text: Both are optimisers: rules that turn a gradient into a step.

slides.notes:
Two optimisers side by side. SGD with momentum uses one learning rate for all parameters and remembers past gradients. Adam also remembers the typical size of each parameter gradient, and uses it to rescale the step for that parameter. That makes Adam forgiving: the default settings often work.

An optimiser is a rule that turns the gradient into a step, and plain gradient descent is the simplest one. Which would you try first on a new problem, and why?

title.text:
Read the loop before you write it:
gradient, then update, repeated

runs.text: for
step
in
range(30):
err = w * xc + b - y
dw = 2 * np.mean(err * xc)
db = 2 * np.mean(err)
w = w - eta * dw
b = b - eta * db

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: err holds the error y-hat - y of every row.
dw and db are the two slopes of the loss: the gradient.
The last two lines are the update rule.
The loop repeats it 30 times. xc is the centred distance.

slides.notes:
Before the lab, read the whole algorithm. This is gradient descent in six lines. The loop runs thirty steps. Inside, the first line computes the error for every row. The next two lines are the two slopes from the formulas, written with numpy means. The last two lines are the update rule, once for w and once for b.

In the lab the notebook gives you the outer frame and you write the four lines for the slopes and the update yourself. In the spreadsheet, each pass through the loop becomes one row.

title.text:
Your lab numbers should
match these at every step

rows.text: w and b after one step with eta = 0.1
Best line by the least squares method of Session 4, on these eight trips

objects.text: If your number differs, find the step that went wrong. Do not change a number to match.

slides.notes:
If your numbers match, carry on. If one does not, stop and look for the step that went wrong, because every later step builds on it. With eta point one, the loss after thirty steps is 0.0819, very close to the least squares answer for the same eight trips, and the weights approach 1.050 and 6.800.

With eta point zero five the loss is 0.1650, still a little behind. With eta point two the loss has grown to about 1762, so that curve is the one that goes up.

title.text:
Lab messages, what they
mean and what to do next

rows.text: The loss is nan or inf
The learning rate is too large and the numbers overflowed
A cell that defines a name was not run
Run all cells from the top
The learning rate is too small, or the loop did not update w
Check that w = w - eta * dw is inside the loop
A row refers to the wrong previous row
Compare with the row above: step t uses row t - 1

slides.notes:
A loss of nan or inf means the learning rate is too large and the numbers blew up, so divide eta by ten. A name error means you skipped a cell, so run all cells from the top. A flat curve means eta is too small or the update sits outside the loop.

In the sheet, a reference error or a zero usually means a row points at the wrong previous row. Python puts the most useful part of an error at the bottom, so read the last line of any message first.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: every training
step ends with an optimiser update

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: every training step ends with an optimiser update

objects.text: Training is one loop, repeated a very large number of times.

runs.text: Forward and backward pass: Session 11. Cross-entropy, the loss for next tokens: Session 17.
Published work uses Adam-type optimisers with warm-up. Product settings are not published.

slides.notes:
Language models of this kind are trained by a loop. Take a batch of text, run the model forward to predict each next token, measure how wrong those predictions were, run backward to get the gradient, and apply an optimiser update. You meet the forward and backward pass properly next session, and the loss for next tokens, called cross-entropy, in Session 17.

The 2017 transformer paper used Adam with four thousand warm-up steps, followed by a decay in proportion to one over the square root of the step number; cosine decay is another common choice. The exact settings of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are not published.

title.text: Exit check: three questions with short answers

rows.text: With eta = 0.1 and a slope of minus 4, what is the new w if the old w is 1?
The loss grows at every step. What is the most likely cause and the fix?
The learning rate is too large. Divide it by 3 or 10.
Give one difference between SGD and Adam.
SGD uses one learning rate for all parameters. Adam rescales the step for each parameter using the typical size of its gradient.

slides.notes:
With a learning rate of point one and a slope of minus four, the new w from an old w of one is one minus point one times minus four, which is one point four. If the loss grows at every step, the learning rate is almost certainly too large, so divide it by three or ten.

And SGD uses a single learning rate for every parameter, while Adam rescales the step for each parameter using the typical size of its gradient. Write your own answers first, then compare.
